definition.def: Evolution is a process of gradual change that takes place over many generations, during which species of animals, plants, or insects slowly change some of their physical characteristics.
examples: ...the evolution of plants and animals. [+ of]
...the theory of evolution by natural selection.

definition.def: Evolution is a process of gradual development in a particular situation or thing over a period of time. [formal]
examples: ...a crucial period in the evolution of modern physics. [+ of]
...an accurate account of his country's evolution.
His long life comprised a series of evolutions.

examples.sentence: Dr Brinkman, a brain researcher at the Australian National University in Canberra, has suggested that evolution of speech went with right-handed preference.
According to Brinkman, as the brain evolved, one side became specialised for fine control of movement (necessary for producing speech) and along with this evolution came right-hand preference.
For the better part of a century, most biologists have been reluctant to use those words, mindful of a principle of evolution that says 'evolution cannot run backwards'.
Not only are evolutionary throwbacks possible, they sometimes play an important role in the forward march of evolution.
In 1890 he proposed that evolution was irreversible: that "an organism is unable to return, even partially, to a previous stage already realised in the ranks of its ancestors".

Early 20th-century biologists came to a similar conclusion, though they qualified it in terms of probability, stating that there is no reason why evolution cannot run backwards - it is just very unlikely.
And so the idea of irreversibility in evolution stuck and came to be known as "Dollo's law".
Since then, so many other examples have been discovered that it no longer makes sense to say that evolution is as good as irreversible.
In 1994, Rudolf Raff and colleagues at Indiana University in the USA decided to use genetics to put a number on the probability of evolution going into reverse.
